explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. Moses, Israel's leader, says, “If you see your brother’s ox or sheep straying, you must not ignore it; be sure to return it to your brother.” (Deuteronomy 22:1) No pretending you didn't see it, no checking your pockets for something to do. I sat in the back of a junk drawer for years, so believe me, a neighbor who stops is a beautiful thing.

explanations.answer: Bring it to the city elders
explanations.explanation: The elders don't come into this one, friend. Moses sends the animal straight back to your brother (Deuteronomy 22:1). No lost-and-found counter, no paperwork, no waiting in line. You see it, you return it.

No priests in this law, friend. Moses doesn't send the animal to anybody but its owner. The text says to return it to your brother (Deuteronomy 22:1). The job lands right on you, the one who spotted it.

explanations.answer: Take it home until he comes for it
explanations.explanation: You've got it, baker. If your brother lives far off or you don't know who he is, the animal goes home with you and stays until he comes seeking it. Then you return it to him (Deuteronomy 22:2). Surprise, you've got a houseguest with hooves! Not a bad deal for a stray, I think.

explanations.answer: Sell it and save the money for him
explanations.explanation: Nobody's running a yard sale here, friend. The text says the animal remains with you until your brother comes seeking it, and then you return it to him (Deuteronomy 22:2). It's the animal he gets back, not an envelope of cash. Keep it fed and wait.

explanations.answer: Turn it loose back into the field
explanations.explanation: That would be ignoring it, friend, and Moses already said you must not (Deuteronomy 22:1). Sending it back out to wander is the opposite of what the law asks. When the owner is far off or unknown, you take the animal home and keep it until he comes seeking it (Deuteronomy 22:2).

True! Moses says to do the same for his donkey, his cloak, “…or anything your brother has lost and you have found.” (Deuteronomy 22:3) That's a wide net, friend. Found a jacket on the road? It's his, not yours. And Moses adds, “…you must not ignore it…”

This one is true, friend. Moses says to do the same for his donkey, his cloak, “…or anything your brother has lost and you have found.” (Deuteronomy 22:3) The word is anything, so the list has no end. If it's your brother's and he lost it, you can't ignore it.

Not quite, friend. Moses says the opposite: when you see your brother's donkey or ox fallen on the road, “…you must not ignore it; you must help him lift it up.” (Deuteronomy 22:4) That's no job for a spectator. Roll up your sleeves, because that ox isn't lifting itself.

False is right, baker. Waiting around isn't an option here. Moses says, “…you must not ignore it; you must help him lift it up.” (Deuteronomy 22:4) So you don't stand there watching a fallen ox and hoping for the best. You get your hands on it and help your brother.
Yes, baker. Moses says whoever does these things “…is detestable to the LORD your God.” (Deuteronomy 22:5) That's the exact word the text uses. I won't add anything to it, because the text doesn't.

Close in sound, friend, but it's not the word Moses uses. He says whoever does these things “…is detestable to the LORD your God.” (Deuteronomy 22:5) Detestable is the word in the text, so that's the one I'll stick with.

Foolish isn't the word on the page, friend. Moses says whoever does these things “…is detestable to the LORD your God.” (Deuteronomy 22:5) That's how the text puts it. I'm not going to soften it or add to it.

explanations.answer: That you may prolong your days
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Moses says to let the mother go “…so that it may be well with you and that you may prolong your days.” (Deuteronomy 22:7) A promise of long life attached to a little bird, friend. I won't guess at the how, because the text doesn't say.

Nothing about flocks increasing here, friend. The mother bird is the one in this law, and the promise Moses gives is “…so that it may be well with you and that you may prolong your days.” (Deuteronomy 22:7) It's about you and your days.

explanations.answer: That your harvest may be great
explanations.explanation: A big harvest would be nice, but it isn't in this verse, friend. Moses says to let the mother go “…so that it may be well with you and that you may prolong your days.” (Deuteronomy 22:7) The promise is well-being and long days. Nothing about crops.

Right, baker. Moses says to build the railing “…so that you do not bring bloodguilt on your house if someone falls from it.” (Deuteronomy 22:8) A railing costs a lot less than a regret, friend. Build it before anybody has to find out why.

Shame is a good guess, friend, but it's not the word. Moses says the railing keeps you from bringing “bloodguilt” on your house if someone falls from it. (Deuteronomy 22:8) That's a heavier word, and it's the one the text uses. Build the railing.

No money talk in this one, friend. Moses says to put up the railing “…so that you do not bring bloodguilt on your house if someone falls from it.” (Deuteronomy 22:8) The word is bloodguilt. A railing is a small cost next to that.

That's right, baker. Moses says “…the young woman’s father and mother shall bring the proof of her virginity to the city elders at the gate” (Deuteronomy 22:15). Both parents speak up for their daughter before the elders. The husband has accused her, and her parents answer him.

Brothers aren't mentioned in this law, friend. The text says her father and mother bring the proof to the city elders at the gate (Deuteronomy 22:15). It's her parents who stand before the elders. This is a heavy part of the speech, so I'll keep it simple.
No priests here, friend. The text says her father and mother bring the proof, and they bring it to the city elders at the gate (Deuteronomy 22:15). The elders are the ones who hear the case.

Yes, baker. The elders “…shall take the man and punish him.” and they fine him a hundred shekels of silver, which goes to the young woman's father. (Deuteronomy 22:18-19) The text says he gave “…a virgin of Israel a bad name.” His accusation costs him.

explanations.answer: Send him out of the city
explanations.explanation: Sending him out of the city isn't part of this law, friend. The elders punish him and fine him a hundred shekels of silver, paid to the young woman's father (Deuteronomy 22:18-19). And she remains his wife. He must not divorce her as long as he lives.

Serving her father isn't what the text says, friend. The elders punish the man and fine him a hundred shekels of silver, and the silver goes to her father (Deuteronomy 22:18-19). That's the penalty the law gives.

Not so, friend. The text says she “…shall remain his wife; he must not divorce her as long as he lives.” (Deuteronomy 22:19) The door to divorce is closed for him. He made the accusation, and he's held to that.
False is right, baker. Moses says she “…shall remain his wife; he must not divorce her as long as he lives.” (Deuteronomy 22:19) After the accusation, he can't just walk away from the marriage.
Not quite, friend. The text says, “…both the man who slept with her and the woman must die.” (Deuteronomy 22:22) It's both of them, not just one. This is a heavy one, so I'll leave it at that.

False is right, baker. Moses says, “…both the man who slept with her and the woman must die.” (Deuteronomy 22:22) The man and the woman are named together. It's a heavy law, and the text is clear on it.

explanations.answer: She did not cry out in the city
explanations.explanation: That's the reason, baker. Moses says both are stoned, “…the young woman because she did not cry out in the city, and the man because he has violated his neighbor’s wife.” (Deuteronomy 22:24) This is a heavy one. Two people, two reasons, and Moses gives each reason plainly.

explanations.answer: She did not tell her family
explanations.explanation: Her family isn't named in the reason, friend. Moses says she is stoned “…because she did not cry out in the city…” (Deuteronomy 22:24) That's the one reason he gives for her, and it's a heavy one.

explanations.answer: She lied to the city elders
explanations.explanation: Lying to the elders doesn't come up, friend. Moses gives this reason for the young woman: “…because she did not cry out in the city…” (Deuteronomy 22:24) The man is stoned for a different reason, because he has violated his neighbor's wife.

True, baker. In the open country Moses says, “…only the man who has done this must die.” (Deuteronomy 22:25) Then he says, “Do nothing to the young woman, because she has committed no sin worthy of death.” (Deuteronomy 22:26) The text is clear about where the blame lies.

It's actually true, friend. Moses says, “…only the man who has done this must die.” (Deuteronomy 22:25) About the young woman he says, “Do nothing to the young woman, because she has committed no sin worthy of death.” (Deuteronomy 22:26) The text is plain.

Yes, baker. Moses says, “This case is just like one in which a man attacks his neighbor and murders him.” (Deuteronomy 22:26) He sets it right beside murder. The woman cried out, and the verse says there was no one to save her (Deuteronomy 22:27). This one is heavy.
Servant isn't the word, friend. The text says the case is “…just like one in which a man attacks his neighbor and murders him.” (Deuteronomy 22:26) Neighbor is what Moses says.
Enemy isn't in the verse, friend. Moses says, “This case is just like one in which a man attacks his neighbor and murders him.” (Deuteronomy 22:26) The word he uses is neighbor.

explanations.answer: He must marry her and never divorce her
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. Along with the fifty shekels of silver, “…she must become his wife because he has violated her. He must not divorce her as long as he lives.” (Deuteronomy 22:29) Two requirements, and both are in that one verse.

explanations.answer: He must leave the city and never return
explanations.explanation: Leaving the city isn't in this law, friend. The text says the man pays the father fifty shekels of silver, and “…she must become his wife because he has violated her.” (Deuteronomy 22:29) He must not divorce her as long as he lives.

explanations.answer: He must serve her father for seven years
explanations.explanation: Seven years of service isn't in this passage, friend. The text says the man pays her father fifty shekels of silver, and “…she must become his wife because he has violated her.” (Deuteronomy 22:29) He must not divorce her as long as he lives.

That's the one, baker. Moses says, “A man is not to marry his father’s wife, so that he will not dishonor his father’s marriage bed.” (Deuteronomy 22:30) That's the closing law of the chapter, and it's about keeping a family's marriage bed honored.

An uncle's daughter isn't mentioned here, friend. The law at the end of the chapter says, “A man is not to marry his father’s wife, so that he will not dishonor his father’s marriage bed.” (Deuteronomy 22:30) It's about the father's wife, so keep your eyes on that.

No widows or clans in this verse, friend. Moses says, “A man is not to marry his father’s wife, so that he will not dishonor his father’s marriage bed.” (Deuteronomy 22:30) That's the one person this law names.
